GIFT performs a token-level geometric analysis, decomposing the distillation gradient into a component \textbf{parallel} to the RL gradient, which measures first-order conflict and provides a \textbf{safety} filter, and a component \textbf{orthogonal} to it, which quantifies novel directional guidance and provides a measure of \textbf{value}. This decomposition yields a principled scoring rule to rank token-level guidance. We combine this with a progressive \textbf{coverage annealing} schedule that shrinks the budget of tokens receiving distillation, ensuring that the most conflicting updates are discarded first while the most complementary ones are retained at full strength. This facilitates a smooth transition from dense, geometrically-filtered guidance to a pure, outcome-grounded objective at convergence. Extensive experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks show that GIFT consistently outperforms strong baselines across multiple model scales, achieving relative gains of up to 9.5\% on difficult mathematical reasoning tasks. papers.title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping

papers.title: A Comprehensive Evaluation on Quantization Techniques for Large Language Models

papers.title: Foreclassing: From Forecasts to Decisions

papers.title: Displacement Moments and Path-Terminal Separation in Brownian Interpolant Sampling
papers.summary: Brownian stochastic interpolants connect paired endpoint samples, yet their sampling error can depend on displacement moments even when neither endpoint has a first moment. For arbitrary Borel couplings, we prove early-stopped, target-to-output KL guarantees for standard Euler sampling from the true source. A fourth displacement moment gives an explicit $O(N^{-1})$ bound; a second moment suffices for fixed-law convergence as drift error vanishes. For one fixed coupling with no displacement moment above two, original bridge-path KL stays of order one, comparison-path KL is of order $1/\log N$, and terminal KL is at most $C/N^2$ on the same grid. The path decomposition identifies the information about the source discarded by Markov projection. When the original bridge is Markov, current-state Euler sampling instead has a second-moment $O((M_2+d)/N)$ bound; finite-entropy Schroedinger bridges for the probability Brownian reference are included. We also construct a current-state learner with expected output KL consistency from iid endpoint pairs. Numerical diagnostics illustrate the distinct errors. Conditional diffusion identities specify a restoration interface, while image controls find no iterative advantage over cheap probabilistic predictors. Uniform terminal rates for general second-moment couplings remain open.

papers.title: An end-to-end framework for uncertainty-aware validation of generative models
papers.summary: Density estimation with generative models is a common task in the physical sciences, for example in background estimation in particle physics. Existing machine learning techniques, however, lack methods to quantify uncertainties that can be propagated into a statistical test. That limits the validation of generative models to standard goodness-of-fit tests, in which the generative model is treated as exact (point-null hypothesis). But a model fitted to a finite training set is never exact, so if its uncertainties are neglected, any sufficiently powerful goodness-of-fit test will eventually reject it once the test set is large enough to resolve this estimation error. We propose SIGMA, an end-to-end framework combining density estimation with principled uncertainty quantification. We use Gaussian mixture models, for which uncertainties are tractable, and further construct a new goodness-of-fit test in which these uncertainties are profiled as nuisance parameters to account for the statistical error of the fit, promoting the conventional point-null test to a composite one. A rejection then signals genuine mismodeling rather than a test set large enough to resolve the error of the fit, provided the propagated uncertainties faithfully cover that error. We demonstrate the framework on a controlled two-dimensional toy model and on a collider physics benchmark modeling the QCD background process. With uncertainties included, the same model can be trusted on test sets up to an order of magnitude larger than the standard test allows. Our work thus provides a statistically grounded basis for a robust use of generative models in the physical sciences.

papers.title: LinMix: Data Mixing as Linear Domain Attribution
papers.summary: Language model performance depends strongly on the mixture of domains in the pretraining data corpus. Popular data mixing methods select these domain weights by training many small proxy models on random mixes and then fitting a regression model to predict performance from the mix. papers.title: Euclidean Crowding-Driven Adaptive Euclidean-Hyperbolic Graph Learning
papers.summary: Hyperbolic graph representation learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling hierarchical data. papers.title: Combinatorial Lock for Trojan-Resilient AI Engines via Hash-Assisted Spectral Filtering
papers.summary: Multi-trigger backdoor attacks, in which heterogeneous trigger mechanisms (e.g., patch, blend, warping, and the latent-domain Spy-Watermark) coexist within a single poisoned model, cannot be addressed by existing shortcut-based defenses that assume a single, static attack mechanism. papers.title: Your Policy Is Secretly a Harness: The Decision Geometry of Agent Interfaces
papers.summary: Language model agents are post-trained and deployed through a harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present a task to the model and execute its outputs. Reversing the order of the observation fields leaves every optimal decision unchanged yet lowers a trained model's success from 85.0% to 19.2%. Conversely, every new harness that a fixed-model comparison rejects but that raises the ceiling outperforms the original agent after further training under it, and ceiling and mismatch measured beforehand predict these gains. For coding-agent harnesses on Terminal-Bench Lite, ceiling minus mismatch estimated with a stronger model as a stand-in for the optimum reproduces the accuracy ranking, while either term alone does not. papers.title: Sharpness-Aware Muon: Matrix-Aware Optimization with Momentum-Guided Perturbations
papers.summary: Muon is a matrix-aware optimizer that combines momentum with orthogonalization to produce structured update directions with strong empirical behavior. However, it only shapes the geometry of the update itself and does not explicitly control neighborhood worst-case loss or bias training toward flat regions, which are often linked to stronger generalization. We then show that this formulation faces an efficiency--stability tension: constructing the perturbation requires an extra gradient evaluation, while the perturbation itself is generated from a single minibatch gradient and is therefore noisy. To resolve this issue, we propose \textsc{MoMuSAM}, which turns Muon's momentum from an update variable into a sharpness-probing signal. By using normalized momentum as the perturbation direction, \textsc{MoMuSAM} removes the extra clean-gradient computation and replaces the single-batch perturbation proxy with a temporally aggregated one. We prove that both \textsc{MuSAM} and \textsc{MoMuSAM} attain the same asymptotic first-order stationarity order, and further show that \textsc{MoMuSAM} yields a more stable stochastic linearization than \textsc{MuSAM}. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that sharpness awareness consistently improves Muon.

papers.title: Manifold meta-learning for reduced-complexity neural system identification

papers.title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination
papers.summary: Lean is increasingly used to verify mathematical proofs and software produced by LLM agents, but writing formal proofs remains hard. Existing prover systems take a divide-and-conquer approach that recursively decomposes hard proof goals into easier lemmas and splits again any lemma that resists proof. However, a lemma can resist proof for different reasons, including insufficient guidance, a false statement, or a flaw in the decomposition that produced it. Existing systems cannot tell these apart as a failed attempt reports little beyond its failure, and responses are confined to the failing node without considering the rest of the proof or revising the plan above it. The system may thus keep decomposing obligations along a flawed proof direction until the budget runs out, causing the whole proof attempt to fail. We introduce Maestro, a Lean prover harness that handles failures through global coordination. Provers report why they failed, not just that they failed, and a coordinator that sees the whole proof chooses an appropriate response, such as guiding a stuck prover, correcting a false lemma, or retracting a flawed subtree and replanning it. The same harness extends to verified code synthesis, where a checked counterexample sends the code back for repair. We evaluate Maestro with four frontier LLMs on seven mathematics and three software verification benchmarks. It proves more targets than each model's native coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) on every benchmark the agent has not already saturated, with the largest gains on research-level mathematics. With Claude Opus 5, it discovers its own proofs of 34 of the 48 theorems in the June 2026 release of arXivLean, against 19 for the native agent. It also outperforms all published prover systems on every benchmark they share, solving 669/672 PutnamBench, 59/60 Lean-IMO-Bench, and 6/6 IMO 2026.

papers.title: In-Context Multi-Operator Learning with DeepOSets
papers.summary: An important application of neural networks in scientific computing is non-linear operator learning. papers.title: Deep Bayesian Approaches for Interpretable Nonlinear Structural System Identification
papers.summary: System identification, namely the inference of mathematical representations of dynamical systems from measured data, is fundamental to engineering diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making. papers.title: Beyond Update Counts: A Control Map for Evaluating Test-Time Model Updates
papers.summary: Test-time updating lets a language model change persistent state after training---such as model weights, adapter parameters, or a memory module---before or while answering queries. For the standard local walk on a $k$-CNF with an assignment that satisfies a majority of each clause, we determine the sharp source threshold $s_*$. Below $s_*$, on some instances a single admissible source forces nontermination however clauses are selected; at $s_*$, with fixed $D$, the expected number of flips is at most cubic in the initial Hamming distance, against linear under independence, with matching worst-case instances; and any fixed margin above $s_*$ restores linear dependence on the distance. Third, verified backtracking for noisy predecessor search remains correct under a sufficiently strong bound on the comparison errors. In every setting the algorithm may also restart, which supplies no fresh randomness; restarting restores exponential tails exactly when the nontermination event has a prefix cover of cost below one.

papers.title: Data-driven Discovery of Lie Symmetries and First Integrals with Latent ODEs
papers.summary: We present LatentLieODE, a novel neural ODE method to discover linear Lie symmetries and first integrals of the learned dynamics from timeseries observations such as video inputs. papers.title: Winner's Curse Drives False Promises in Data-Driven Decisions
papers.summary: A major challenge in data-driven decision-making is accurate policy evaluation---i.e., guaranteeing that a learned decision-making policy achieves the promised benefits. A popular strategy is model-based policy evaluation, which estimates a model from data to infer counterfactual outcomes. This strategy is known to produce unwarrantedly optimistic estimates of the true benefit due to the winner's curse. We searched the recent literature on data-driven decision-making, identifying a sample of 55 papers published in Management Science in the past decade; all but two relied on this flawed methodology. Several common justifications are provided: (1) the estimated models are accurate, stable, and well-calibrated, (2) the historical data uses random treatment assignment, (3) the model family is well-specified, and (4) the evaluation methodology uses sample splitting. Unfortunately, we show that no combination of these justifications avoids the winner's curse. First, we provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that the winner's curse can cause large, spurious reported benefits even when all these justifications hold. Second, we perform a simulation study based on the recent and consequential data-driven refugee matching problem. We construct a synthetic refugee matching environment (calibrated to closely match the real setting) but designed so that no assignment policy can improve expected employment compared to random assignment. Model-based methods report large, stable gains of around 60% even when the true effect is zero; these gains are on par with improvements of 22-75% reported in the literature. Our results provide strong evidence against model-based evaluation.

papers.title: Alignment via Generalization
papers.summary: AI systems can become better at achieving the goals we give them without becoming better at doing what we actually want. Studying this alignment problem rigorously requires a framework connecting measurable performance to intended behavior. papers.title: Can a Teenager Fool an AI? Evaluating Low-Cost Cosmetic Attacks on Age Estimation Systems
papers.summary: Age estimation systems are increasingly deployed as gatekeepers for age-restricted online content, yet their robustness to cosmetic modifications has not been systematically evaluated. papers.title: Adaptive Estimation and Inference in Conditional Moment Models via the Discrepancy Principle

papers.title: Anatomy of a Scam Call: What 10,000 real scam and spam calls reveal about how phone scammers operate
papers.summary: Telephone fraud is pervasive and costly, but its inner workings are rarely observed at scale. papers.title: Min-Marginal Power Indices for Multi-Objective Feature Selection
papers.summary: Game-theoretic feature selection scores each feature by its average marginal contribution across coalitions. An average shows whether a feature helps overall, but not whether, in some coalition, adding it turns an acceptable model into an unacceptable one. Building on minimum marginal aggregation, we define the Min-Marginal Power Index (MinPI) on a binary utility-threshold game. For a fixed quota, MinPI takes the value -1, 0, or +1 and labels each feature harmful, neutral, or decisive. A harmful label carries its own evidence, an evaluated coalition in which adding the feature drops utility below the quota, so no score cutoff is needed; finite-budget estimators keep this property but may miss harmful features. We use MinPI to propose feature removals, which are accepted only if they pass a validation gate, and to prefilter multi-objective search. On six benchmark datasets over five seeds, MinPI removed 12.5% of analyzed features with almost no loss of held-out utility. On Madelon and Abalone, where it removed the most, its removals cost far less held-out utility than random removals of the same size. Prefiltering increased the dataset-averaged hypervolume of multi-objective search in all five seeds. MinPI is therefore a conservative feature-deletion step whose gains are largest where the data contain many removable features.

papers.title: When is early stopping beneficial under label noise? A phase diagram for kernel gradient flow
papers.summary: Early stopping is commonly used to prevent fitting label noise from degrading generalization. Does this mean that, when a positive fraction of the training labels is intrinsically unpredictable, the best test error must occur before interpolation? Experiments on a CIFAR10 classification task with randomly labeled examples motivate the opposite possibility: although fixed-feature and shallow models exhibit late-time deterioration of the test error, the need for early stopping essentially disappears in larger, deeper convolutional networks even after the random labels have all been classified correctly. We determine when late-time deterioration disappears entirely in a solvable setting. For kernel gradient flow on a synthetic noisy classification task, we derive sharp high-dimensional learning curves and obtain a phase diagram controlled by the balance between the linear kernel component that learns the shared relation between inputs and labels and the higher-order components that enable fitting the label noise. In one regime, generalization is optimized at finite time and early stopping is necessary. In another, generalization improves until interpolation, but the endpoint is suboptimal across kernels. At the boundary, the interpolating endpoint attains the lowest generalization error across the considered kernel family and all training times. Thus, even with extensive irreducible label noise, interpolation can outperform early stopping. The neural-network experiments leave open how learned representations acquire an analogous favorable geometry.

papers.title: Grounding on Request: Learning Modality Control in Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: When an image and its caption disagree, can a user reliably control which one a vision-language model (VLM) follows? Finally, we test our method on real-world news video and find that visual control improves when the relevant evidence is made easier to access. papers.title: Accelerating LLM Pre-Training through Flat-Direction Dynamics Enhancement

papers.title: Necessary but Not Sufficient: Temperature Control and Reproducibility in LLM-as-Judge Safety Evaluations

papers.title: Cost-aware Bayesian Optimization via the Pandora's Box Gittins Index

papers.title: Holo-NN: Holographic Nearest Neighbor Search via Compressive Sensing
papers.summary: In the age of AI, privacy-preserving approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search over high-dimensional embeddings has emerged as a critical yet frustratingly challenging domain, dominated by tradeoffs between speed, privacy, and accuracy. papers.title: From Dueling Bandits to Episodic MDPs: Learning with Adversarial Preference Feedback
papers.summary: In dueling bandits, the learner compares two arms in each round and observes only which one is preferred. papers.title: LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders
papers.summary: Location encoders map geographic coordinates to high-dimensional descriptors through contrastive alignment with paired Earth Observation imagery. We prove that this construction is structurally limited: any Lipschitz location encoder produces an output of intrinsic dimension at most 2, regardless of architecture or bandwidth, which forces the contrastive loss to strictly exceed its asymptotic optimum. Empirically, joint training also collapses the encoder's embedding covariance to low rank. Although dimension-limited, current location encoders sidestep this spectral collapse by training against a frozen image encoder, which we reinterpret as a covariance regularizer that supplies a high-rank target for the location encoder to fold onto. However, extending this approach to multimodal inputs is challenging, as location encoders should simultaneously map a single location to multiple, potentially incompatible, descriptors. We identify two requirements a regularizer must satisfy for location encoding in multimodal regimes: co-alignment across modalities, since adapters alone cannot align independently pretrained encoders; and high effective rank, since the location encoder inherits its target's spectrum. We propose LoCA (Location Contrastive Alignment), a two-stage pipeline that satisfies both. Stage 1 jointly trains Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders with contrastive learning, producing a co-aligned, high-rank multimodal target. Stage 2 freezes the image encoders and trains a location and a tabular metadata encoder as projection adapters with multi-view contrastive learning. Against five state-of-the-art encoders on 17 tasks ranging from land cover and wildfire forecasting to geophysical, socio-economic, biodiversity and climate applications, LoCA achieves the most task wins, is the only model to outperform every other on a majority of tasks, and wins 68.8% of all per-task comparisons.

papers.title: Fully quantum training of parametric circuits with Quantum Hamiltonian Descent
papers.summary: Parametric quantum circuits are usually trained by classical, local optimizers, which use the quantum computer only to evaluate the cost function, or its gradient, one point at a time. Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) takes a different route: in this quantum algorithm for continuous optimization, the parameters become the position of a quantum particle, with the cost function as its potential, and two time schedules control kinetic and potential energy so that the wavefunction explores the whole landscape and tunnels towards the global minimum. QHD, however, assumes a classically computable cost function, and its digital implementation is poorly understood: standard error bounds grow exponentially with the number of qubits per parameter, and the schedules are borrowed from classical optimization. Here we propose to train parametric circuits with QHD entirely on the quantum computer, through an online step in which the qubits encoding the parameters coherently control the circuit on a second register. We prove that, for cost functions with a smooth periodic extension, including those of parametric circuits, the simulation error admits a bound independent of the grid resolution, and that for circuits the bound grows at most linearly with the number of parameters. We also show that the ideal dynamics depends on the two schedules only through a single curve, which controls the adiabaticity of the search, and that the remaining freedom can be used to minimize the gate count. Simulations on benchmark functions and parametric circuits show that, at equal cost, schedules designed in this way markedly increase the probability of finding the global minimum.

papers.title: Constitution-Guided Watermarking
papers.summary: Regulation such as the EU AI Act requires providers of language models to mark generated text in a machine-readable way. Watermarking meets this requirement by embedding a secret-key signal during generation, so the provider can later detect its model's text. A watermark should stay detectable, preserve quality and survive paraphrasing, but a stronger signal survives more paraphrasing and distorts more text. Providers resolve this trade-off with one configuration for all requests, although a provider may want robustness for misuse-prone requests and no watermark for editing assistance, which the EU AI Act exempts. We introduce \emph{constitution-guided watermarking}, in which the provider states these requirements as natural-language rules, a \emph{watermark constitution}, and each request receives its rule's configuration. Offline, a reasoning agent reads the rules and the watermark code and refines each rule's configuration from measured detection, quality and robustness. At deployment, a monitor routes each prompt to its rule's configuration without modifying the serving model. Each configuration is stored with its evidence, so the provider can audit every deployment decision, including unmet requirements. Our evaluation with the KGW watermark shows that (i) on misuse-prone requests, the framework detects more paraphrased text than fixed configurations and random search at matching clean detection and quality, (ii) it exempts all editing requests, and (iii) changing the stated priorities shifts the selected configuration as intended.

papers.title: Amortized Thompson Sampling and Efficient Information-Directed Sampling for Simulator-Based Design
papers.summary: Thompson sampling is a widely used strategy for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, offering a principled way to balance exploration and exploitation. This strategy involves maximizing a target objective under a single sample drawn from the current belief over unknown quantities. Conventionally, this optimization is performed once the belief has been inferred from data, and it becomes computationally burdensome when many Thompson samples are required, especially in continuous action spaces. In this work, we introduce an approach that amortizes this process ahead of time, before any data is collected, so that an approximation of the full Thompson sampling distribution is available immediately once observations arrive. We employ this approach to solve the multi-round setting, involving sequential data acquisition and Thompson-sample recommendation across rounds. Beyond accelerating Thompson sampling, our approach enables efficient estimation of expected information gain about the optimal action. This can be used to select more informative Thompson samples or to obtain maximally informative designs with optimization. Combining this estimate of expected information gain with immediate regret supports information-directed sampling (IDS), which can outperform Thompson sampling by explicitly balancing these two quantities. We demonstrate our approach on two simulator-based design problems in synthetic biology, where the simulators have intractable likelihoods.

It also improves general utility over the vanilla models while maintaining comparable over-refusal behavior. Our results show that the safety of a LoopLM cannot be inferred from a single recurrent depth, motivating safety alignment across recurrent computation. papers.title: Iterative Policy Optimization: Batch-Online Multi-Turn RL via Single-Turn RL
papers.summary: Practical LLM agents often operate over multi-turn conversations where success is determined only after the full interaction ends. Most multi-turn RL methods train via on-policy rollouts, but unlike in single-turn RL, the policy cannot produce a trajectory alone, since an external environment must respond after each agent turn. For conversational agents, this environment is a user, but real users are generally unavailable inside the training loop and simulated users are difficult to build faithfully. Separately, real-world deployment is rarely fully online or fully offline. The common production pattern is called batch online, where the current policy is deployed to collect a batch of interaction data, then retrained on that batch and redeployed. We show that this batch-online setting creates an opportunity for applying the classical approximate policy iteration algorithm. Our central observation is that running standard token-level, single-turn GRPO with a learned turn-level $Q$-function as the reward model is a policy improvement step for the multi-turn problem. Building on this, we present Iterative Policy Optimization (IterPO), which alternates between fitting $Q^π$ from logged Monte Carlo returns via standard reward modeling (policy evaluation) and running single-turn GRPO against $Q^π$ (policy improvement). During policy improvement, the learned $Q^π$ scores candidate responses by their expected downstream return, avoiding the need for simulator rollouts of the remaining conversation. Overall, this allows us to do principled multi-turn RL using only single-turn RL methods without an interactive environment or user simulator inside the training loop. papers.title: Neural Disjunctive Normal Forms for Learning Exact Rank Filters

papers.title: EVOLVE: Uncertainty-Aware Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Prediction with Adaptive Prototype Memories
papers.summary: Unsupervised multivariate time series anomaly prediction (AP) aims to estimate future anomaly risks from current observations, providing early-warning signals for proactive intervention and maintenance in complex systems. Existing unsupervised AP methods follow a perturbation-based paradigm, where predefined or random perturbations are injected into historical windows to simulate abnormal future evolution. However, these methods share perturbations across different variables and contexts, and learn deterministic history-to-future evolution. In reality, anomaly evolution is variable- and context-dependent: the same perturbation may be amplified into abnormal future dynamics in one variable or context, while being absorbed as normal fluctuation in another. In addition, future evolution is not uniquely determined by a historical window, since similar histories may lead to multiple plausible trajectories, such as gradual degradation or abrupt changes. To address these problems, we propose EVOLVE, a unified framework that models unsupervised AP via variable- and context-conditioned perturbations and uncertainty-aware future reasoning. EVOLVE constructs context-specific anomaly perturbations through an adaptive anomaly prototype memory, which can dynamically update and retrieve relevant perturbations at the variable level. EVOLVE models uncertainty by sampling multiple latent historical states and decoding through complementary smooth and deviation-amplifying evolution hypotheses, and the disagreement among decoded future trajectories is used to estimate future anomaly risk. Extensive experiments on six real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that EVOLVE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art anomaly prediction baselines.

papers.title: SAUSS: Stochastic Approximation with Unbiased Simulated Scores for Limited Dependent Variable Models

papers.title: Strictly Replicable Realizable Learning: Unknown Marginals, Finite-Class Interpolation, and the Cost of Shared Randomness
papers.summary: Strict replicability requires two independent training samples, processed with the same random seed, to produce exactly the same hypothesis. papers.title: Beyond Best-of-$k$: Prior-Consistent DAPS for Ambiguous Nonlinear Inverse Problems
papers.summary: Diffusion models have become strong priors for solving inverse problems. However, nonlinear inverse problems such as phase retrieval remain challenging when multiple measurement-consistent solutions are distinguishable only by the prior; we call such measurements ambiguous. Existing diffusion-based samplers rely on local approximations during reconstruction. For an ambiguous measurement, these approximations can allow measurement guidance to favor a measurement-consistent mode that is close to a prior-supported mode but is itself not supported by the prior. Evaluation often masks this type of failure by reporting the best-of-$k$ runs, where the best is selected by comparison to the ground truth. We introduce Prior-Consistent DAPS (PC-DAPS), a variant of Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling (DAPS) designed to address this failure case by maintaining multiple candidate solutions within a single sampling run. As annealing noise decreases, PC-DAPS prunes and replaces weaker candidates according to their prior consistency, without any ground-truth access. PC-DAPS reduces the incidence of prior-inconsistent samples and improves sample quality on nonlinear inverse problems while preserving sample quality and diversity on linear inverse problems.

papers.title: When Does Self-Supervised Pretraining Help Tabular Models? A Study of Label Scarcity and Missing Data

papers.title: Evaluating the Applicability of LLM Inference Optimizations on Apple Silicon

papers.title: Parallel gradient boosting for flexible estimation of conditional distributions
papers.summary: Boosting is one of the most successful learning techniques for standard classification and regression tasks. Its extension to multi-output prediction problems has found an increasing number of applications in recent years. Among them is the prediction of entire conditional distributions rather than single functionals, which can often be framed as a multi-output regression problem, for example multiple quantile regression. Addressing such problems with classical implementations of boosting is computationally challenging, because usually one base model is trained for each target at every iteration. More efficient variants of boosting have been proposed to speed up training, but they tend to be tied to specific loss functions and classes of base learners, usually decision trees. In this work, we study a modification of the gradient boosting algorithm, which we call parallel gradient boosting, designed to circumvent all these limitations. The core idea is to use a common descent direction for all training observations. By doing so, only one base model is needed at each iteration, regardless of the number of targets, which allows for considerable performance gains. We establish sufficient conditions for the convergence of the algorithm, whose practical use is introduced via the multiple quantile regression setting. We show that in such a setting, it provides predictions of similar quality to state-of-the-art boosting libraries such as XGBoost, while being faster by several orders of magnitude. Then, we evaluate the properties of the resulting conditional distribution estimator, which is shown empirically to outperform other nonparametric and semiparametric estimators, especially in high-dimensional settings and in the presence of mixed and/or missing covariates.

papers.title: Drift Says When, Budget Says How Much: Rate-Controlled KV Re-selection for Long-Form Multimodal Generation
papers.summary: KV cache compression for multimodal LLMs usually selects the visual tokens to keep once, at prefill, and reuses that selection for the whole generation. papers.title: UnlearningSoup: Is Repeated Tuning Necessary for Large Language Model Unlearning?
papers.summary: Large language models trained on vast corpora inherently risk memorizing harmful content that may later re-emerge in their outputs. To mitigate this issue, existing unlearning methods typically rely on training-based parameter updates, such as gradient ascent and its variants, to delete targeted content while preserving other knowledge. To address this challenge, we investigate whether unlearning runs exhibit exploitable structure in weight space, and observe that models from different runs still lie in a shared evaluation-performance basin. This suggests that stronger models may be recovered through an unlearning-tailored soup strategy, reducing the need for repeated tuning for further improvement or new settings. Motivated by this, we propose UnlearningSoup, a unified framework that provides two strategies: EfficientSoup uses binary-search-based interpolation to quickly discover a well-performing model in the early stage, where repeated tuning would otherwise make strong model selection costly. PerformanceSoup uses reweighted souping to efficiently unlock the remaining performance potential in the later stage, where repeated tuning becomes increasingly inefficient. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and models show that UnlearningSoup delivers 2.4x to 3.3x efficiency gains in hyperparameter selection, while consistently improving performance across settings.

papers.title: Is High Local Accuracy Enough? Geometric Consensus with Support-Adaptive Statistical Personalization for Federated Learning
papers.summary: Real-world deployment of personalized federated learning (PFL) requires adapting to heterogeneous clients while preserving recognition performance beyond local distributions. However, high local accuracy can conceal failures on locally rare or absent classes. Effective personalization should therefore strengthen global recognition while raising the personalization floor. We propose an evaluation protocol that complements local accuracy with global, rare-class, and unseen-class evaluations to reveal generalization obscured by local scores, and assesses personalization floors among the worst-performing clients to expose weaknesses hidden by aggregate performance. To meet these deployment challenges, we propose FedGRC, a unified PFL framework integrating generalization and personalization through (i) Consensus-Guided Representation Learning (CGRL), which learns discriminative representations through shared directional and magnitude guidance; (ii) Multilayer Metric Synthesis (MMS), which constructs a shared covariance metric from these multilayer representations for statistical classification; and (iii) Support-Adaptive Shrinkage Personalization (SASP), which adapts class means within this metric by shrinking local estimates toward shared means according to local sample support, enabling adaptation while retaining shared knowledge. Extensive experiments, including benchmarking against 21 methods across 5 heterogeneity settings on 3 datasets and comprehensive ablation studies, validate the effectiveness of FedGRC. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, FedGRC surpasses state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines in global recognition and personalization floors by at least 2.17% and 2.13%, respectively. On the real-world heterogeneous FedRS dataset, it outperforms the respective best baselines by 2.15%, 3.30%, and 4.61% in local adaptation, global recognition, and the personalization floor.

papers.title: Few-shot Classification as Multi-instance Verification: Effective Backbone-agnostic Transfer across Domains
papers.summary: We investigate cross-domain few-shot learning under the constraint that fine-tuning of backbones (i.e., feature extractors) is impossible or infeasible---a scenario that is increasingly common in practical use cases---and show how representing few-shot classification as a series of multiple instance verification (MIV) tasks enables competitive classification performance using the static embeddings produced by frozen, "black-box" backbones. More specifically, based on this novel representation, we introduce a new approach to few-shot domain adaptation named the "MIV-head": a classification head that is backbone-agnostic and computationally efficient. We show that the core components of the MIV-head, when trained on few-shot data from a target domain, collectively yield strong performance on test data from that domain. Importantly, they do so without fine-tuning the backbone, requiring only the "meta-testing" phase. In experiments under various settings on an extension of the Meta-Dataset benchmark for cross-domain few-shot image classification, using representative off-the-shelf convolutional neural network and vision transformer backbones pretrained on ImageNet1K, we demonstrate that the MIV-head achieves highly competitive accuracy when compared to state-of-the-art "adapter" (or "partial fine-tuning") methods applied to the same backbones, while incurring substantially lower adaptation cost. Moreover, compared to our approach, well-known "classification head" approaches achieve a substantially lower level of accuracy. We share our code at: https://github.com/xxweka/MIV-head.

papers.title: POI Recommendation with LLM-Augmented Multi-Graph Learning and Contrastive Alignment
papers.summary: Point-of-interest (POI) recommendation models based on graph neural networks achieve strong performance by propagating collaborative signals over user-item interactions, yet they struggle with the cold-start problem, where items with few or no interactions are not represented. In this paper, we propose LLM-augmented Multi-Graph Contrastive Learning (LLM-MGCL), a multi-graph neural network that uses semantic and spatial information about items to extend the LightGCN backbone with two auxiliary item-item graphs: a semantic graph constructed from sentence embeddings of LLM-generated photo summaries and keywords, and a geographic graph derived from Haversine distances between business locations. Item embeddings are propagated over all three graphs in parallel, fused additively, and aligned across views through a bidirectional InfoNCE contrastive objective that connects behavioral, semantic, and spatial representations of the same items. Experiments on the Yelp Multimodal Recommendation Dataset show that LLM-MGCL outperforms classical collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, and non-contrastive graph neural network baselines. It improves Recall@20 by 48.5% and NDCG@20 by 59.0% over LightGCN, while trailing the strongest contrastive baseline, Self-supervised Graph Learning (SGL), slightly in aggregate. A popularity-stratified evaluation shows that LLM-MGCL achieves the highest recall on cold and warm items, whereas SGL remains better on popular items. An ablation study reveals that the cross-view contrastive alignment (CA) is the primary driver of the aggregate gains. Our results suggest that externally grounded, LLM-derived item knowledge can partially compensate for missing collaborative signal and mitigate the item cold-start problem in POI recommendation.

papers.title: nnInteractive Agent: General-Purpose AI Agents as 3D Image Annotators
papers.summary: Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it. Asked for 'the muscles used for chewing', an agent identifies and segments the masseters and pterygoids; asked to count liver lesions, it writes its own code to find candidates and splits a merged lesion on request. Our open-source nninteractive-agent provides nnInteractive as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), together with a skill that encodes how experienced users prompt it. On a benchmark spanning CT, MRI, PET and micro-CT of humans, a mouse and an ant (14 images; 51 targets from organs and tumours to muscles, foot bones, vessel trees and an insect brain), Claude Code and Codex reach a mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from the request alone; when told where each target is, both reach 0.85 and prompt nearly as effectively as an oracle that places prompts using the reference segmentation. A text-prompted 3D model (VoxTell) is more accurate on most standard radiological targets but less robust: it returns an empty mask for one of them and fails on the leg muscles, the foot bones, the mouse and the ant, where the agents remain accurate. papers.title: NN-Based Transistor Modeling for Ultra-Fast SPICE Simulation and Standard Cell Library Characterization
papers.summary: Neural network (NN)-based transistor models have proven to be a promising solution to accelerate device modeling. Although these models demonstrated remarkable speedup in circuit simulations, they were not rigorously tested in complex tasks within standard EDA tool flows for chip design, which require very high transistor model precision to provide accurate results and converge properly. To investigate their full potential and promise, we develop NN-based transistor models that accurately predict the drain current and various charges for a 3nm nanosheet, and employ the models for a standard cell library characterization. This enables us to evaluate the accuracy and speedup under a very wide range of SPICE simulations, benchmarking our models against an industry-standard implementation. Since standard cell library characterization involves thousands of SPICE simulations, it serves as a great benchmark for transistor model quality and consistency. To further evaluate model accuracy, we also perform analog- and digital-level simulations for various complex circuits. Our experiments reveal that NN-based models are a valid alternative to existing transistor compact models, capable of producing accurate delay and power estimates with a much higher speed and convergence time compared to the conventional Verilog-A-based industry-standard (BSIM-CMG) transistor compact model. Our NNs achieve sub-0.11% and 0.76% errors for delay and total power evaluation on a wide range of circuits, while taking up to 8 times less time during the standard cell library characterization. Additionally, we provide comprehensive information and guidance on NN accuracy, unveiling the relationship between NN size and its effect on circuit simulation precision.

papers.title: XALIGN: A Human-centric Visual Analytics Approach to Understanding AI Explanations
papers.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) methods are usually evaluated for technical properties such as faithfulness and robustness. In high-stakes application domains, experts also need to check model predictions against established knowledge. Different explanation methods often disagree, and this disagreement is hard to see when each method is inspected separately. We propose XALIGN, a visual analytics workflow and interface that shows rule-based explanations and several feature attribution methods (TreeSHAP, KernelSHAP, and LIME) side by side for the same Random Forest model. Agreements and contradictions between the methods become visible signals that users can explore and compare with domain knowledge. We apply XALIGN in two case studies: the German Credit dataset and a meteorological dataset, in which events derived from ICON model output and Cloudnet observations are classified. In both, the views reveal discrepancies between the rule-based explanation and the attribution methods that a single method would not show. In an expert evaluation with three specialists, participants found XALIGN useful for identifying influential features and for avoiding over-trust in predictions. Linking rules to attributions was harder for the participant without an XAI background.

papers.title: EEG-Captioner: Grounding EEG-to-Language Generation in Fundamental Signal Properties
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG)-to-language models offer a promising approach for translating complex neural signals into human-readable descriptions. papers.title: Joint or Per-Option? Compact Encoders for Closed-Set Decisions from 17 Million to 1 Billion Parameters
papers.summary: Many language-model pipelines end in a closed-set decision, such as selecting a tool. Prompting a large language model for it is slow and order-sensitive. We ask how small an encoder for such decisions can be and whether it should read the options jointly or separately. In a three-seed study at 32 million parameters, per-option scoring beats joint scoring on a held-out sample of a 37-benchmark decision suite by 5.8 points of chance-corrected skill at matched optimizer steps and by 2.8 at approximately matched training compute; two external benchmarks agree, though not significantly on their unseen tasks. Crossing reader with initialisation shows that the advantage requires a reranker initialisation, whose query-candidate pair input matches per-option reading; from the raw encoder the two readers are indistinguishable. Per-option scoring needs 5 to 13 times more encoder passes: at most twice the median latency, but more than four times the mean. Of six released joint encoders (17 million to 1 billion parameters), the 68- and 150-million-parameter models exceed a 435-million-parameter DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot classifier by 4.9 and 5.9 accuracy points on 209 overlap-audited System1-Arena tasks and are at least on par with it on the 145 tasks unseen in training. The smallest answers a median request in 14 milliseconds on 16 processor threads, against 728 for the classifier. Reordering options changes 12 to 23% of the joint models' answers (per-option scoring: none). Up to 68 million parameters, they lead their size range on a public leaderboard's private, mainly in-distribution tests.

papers.title: Energy and Latency First: How Deployment Constraints Reverse Time-Series Model Selection
papers.summary: AI models, and time-series models in particular are typically ranked by accuracy and deployed under constraints absent from that ranking. In this paper, we study a real setting where these constraints are explicit and measurable: handover pre- diction in cellular networks, where inference runs on the User Equipment once per 40 ms measurement period and must complete before the network acts. The timing bound is hard: a late prediction is superseded by the measurement it was predicting, while energy is a cumulative budget spent for the life of the device. Neither appears in the objective these models are selected on. We evaluate eight architectures under a protocol that screens for deadline feasibility at the tail rather than the mean, then ranks the feasible models on measured inference energy, count- ing the feature computation that precedes the forward pass and is usually omitted. Gradient-boosted trees on handcrafted temporal features are the most accurate model (F1=0.974) and among the cheapest to run, while the neural architecture an accuracy-only benchmark would rank first (CNN-1D, F1=0.914) costs over 3 times more energy per inference under a realistic duty-cycled deployment pattern. We give three conditions under which this outcome should be expected, so the finding applies beyond telecommunications. Accuracy-only benchmarking does not merely under-report deployment cost. It can rank first a model that cannot be deployed.

papers.title: Redundancy Meets Synergy: Dependency-aware Expert Selection for MoE via Submodular Optimization
papers.summary: While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models effectively scale model capacity through sparse activation, their deployment is often bottlenecked by prohibitive memory requirements. Extracting a compact subset of experts presents a promising solution. However, existing expert selection heuristics predominantly rely on Top-$k$ ranking, which isolates the evaluation of individual experts and ignores the intricate inter-expert dependencies introduced by the MoE gating network. In this paper, we propose DS-MoE, a theoretically grounded framework that redefines expert selection via difference-of-submodular (DS) optimization. By analyzing the second-order Taylor expansion of the loss degradation, we reveal functional duality within expert combinations: redundancy (where experts encode overlapping representations) and synergy (where experts provide complementary error cancellation). To navigate this duality, we mathematically decouple redundancy reduction from synergy maximization by formulating the selection objective as a DS function. Furthermore, we devise a tailored majorization-minimization (MM) algorithm with provable guarantees to efficiently identify a high-quality expert subset. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DS-MoE effectively preserves indispensable expert combinations, achieving superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: ReDence: A Hybrid Agentic and Decision-Model Framework for Rapid, Evidence-Grounded Detection of Modern Social Engineering Scams
papers.summary: Detecting online social engineering (SE) scams often requires examining website workflows, verifying claims against external sources, and connecting evidence across multiple pages. Existing detectors provide limited support for these investigations, leaving analysts to manually gather and validate evidence, which inevitably delays detection and subsequent takedown of these attacks. To address this gap, we present ReDence, an open-source hybrid framework for adaptive, evidence-grounded detection across diverse SE scam categories. ReDence combines two locally hosted models with complementary responsibilities: a fine-tuned multimodal agentic Investigator (Qwen3.5-4B) that performs investigative planning, evidence interpretation, and reporting, and a specialized Decider (Tev1) that handles binary and multiple-choice tasks, including browser-action selection, evidence assessment, and decisions about whether to continue an investigation. By delegating discrete decisions to a specialized model, ReDence reduces reliance on lengthy language-model responses, while preserving the reasoning capabilities required for complex investigations. Our evaluation demonstrates that ReDence achieves 96\% accuracy in detecting scams across twelve SE scam categories, substantially outperforming existing detectors while being at least four times faster than comparable agentic models without compromising investigative depth. ReDence also produces structured, evidence-grounded reports that document investigative actions, supporting and contradictory evidence, and collected artifacts, which allow analysts to independently audit detection decisions and utilize the collected evidence to support subsequent mitigation and takedown efforts.

papers.title: Same molecule, Different Knowledge: Cross-Identifier Binding Failures in LLMs For chemistry
papers.summary: Chemical AI workflows routinely represent the same molecule through multiple co-referring identifiers, including trivial names, IUPAC names, and SMILES, implicitly assuming that these representations provide interchangeable access to an LLM's knowledge. To test this assumption, we first introduce a controlled benchmark and show that it does not hold. Across foundation models spanning 7B to 72B parameters, even chemistry-specialized models, co-referring molecular identifiers consistently expose different subsets of the model's knowledge. We then conduct a series of controlled behavioral, representational, and causal analyses to characterize this failure. We show that even when a model can identify a molecule from its SMILES and retrieve a fact through the corresponding name, the same fact can remain inaccessible directly from SMILES. We term this phenomenon \emph{cross-identifier binding failure}. Further analysis of internal representations, conflicting identifiers, and parameter editing shows that neither improved chemical representation competence nor modification of individual facts is sufficient to establish reliable access across identifiers. Together, these results indicate that the core failure lies in the binding between an identifier and knowledge already present in the model. Motivated by this diagnosis, we introduce Binding Self-Distillation, a simple mitigation that uses lexical identity during training to transfer the model's existing knowledge access to the structural route. This enables factual retrieval directly from SMILES at inference time, without requiring a name lookup or training the underlying model from scratch.

papers.title: Towards Adversarially Robust Multigraph Neural Networks for Financial Crime Analysis
papers.summary: Financial transaction networks are naturally represented as multigraphs, where repeated transactions between the same pair of accounts are modeled as distinct edges. Recently proposed multigraph neural network architectures leverage this structure explicitly to achieve a strong performance on anti-money laundering (AML) tasks. However, their robustness to adversaries that manipulate transaction structures to evade detection remains largely unexplored. We present the first scalable framework for structural attacks and adversarial training of multigraph neural networks using node-edge incidence matrices, adapting projected gradient descent and projected randomized block coordinate descent methods to optimize structural perturbations over such matrices. We further introduce a cycle-based regularizer that penalizes changes in the global counts of directed 2- and 3-cycles, providing a structural measure of attack plausibility. Experiments on synthetic pattern-detection and realistic AML datasets show that our learned attacks substantially outperform non-learnable perturbation baselines in reducing detection performance (PR-AUC), while adversarial training consistently improves robustness against these attacks. These results demonstrate that multigraph neural networks are vulnerable to learned structural attacks and that adversarial training provides an effective defense. Our code is available at https://github.com/denheijmans/robust_multignn.

papers.title: Continuous-depth Deep Gaussian Processes
papers.summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are appealing Bayesian regression models, but their standard discrete-depth parameterization often becomes harder to optimize as depth grows. We argue that depth is better treated as a latent continuous evolution than as a long discrete stack. We therefore propose a continuous-depth formulation in which the latent representation follows a stochastic differential equation with a depth-indexed drift family equipped with a GP-based prior. This reframes the core design choice as the prior placed on that family, rather than adopting a purely neural continuous-depth parameterization as in neural ODE or neural SDE models. We study two instantiations of this idea: CDGP, a direct GP prior over the state--depth drift, and FlowDGP, a flow-evolved prior that captures richer depth dependence at lower training cost. To motivate the redesign, we analyze how the single-sample DGP objective can become increasingly sensitive under repeated layer composition, while residual DGP is a useful first repair that still remains a finite discrete construction. We also give pathwise sensitivity analysis for the continuous-depth formulation. Experiments on synthetic, benchmark, and large-scale regression tasks show that residual DGP improves over plain DGP, while CDGP and FlowDGP provide a stronger overall story across the regimes we study.

papers.title: Is spectral predictability enough? Testing Ω-matching for synthetic pretraining under distribution shift
papers.summary: Synthetic pretraining under distribution shift requires deciding what synthetic data to use. A natural criterion is to match the spectral predictability $Ω$ of the source to the target, but is $Ω$ sufficient? We test this hypothesis, which we call predictability-aware pretraining, across three architectures (LSTM, PatchTST, TCN) and three seeds. Under ideal synthetic-to-synthetic conditions, $Ω$-matched pretraining can outperform even an oracle baseline (+46.8% MSE reduction, LSTM), though the benefit is already architecture-dependent. On the real-world ETTm1 benchmark, however, this relationship does not hold: sine-plus-noise pretraining at matched $Ω$ yields only a marginal mean improvement +2.3% averaged over all three architectures, up to +65.5% on individual channels), whereas $Ω$ matched chaotic ODE trajectories systematically degrade performance -13.2%). The two sources agree on the direction of transfer for only 53% of configurations across all three architectures (Pearson r=-0.02), indicating that $Ω$ carries little information about which source will transfer beneficially. We further observe an architecture-dependent asymmetry in the response to the direction of the $Ω$ gap. We conclude that $Ω$ matching can help in controlled settings but is not sufficient to predict transfer across sources, and we discuss additional signal properties that a source-selection criterion may need to consider.

papers.title: Gandalf: Flash Shall Not Die! Increasing Flash Storage Lifetime for KV Cache Offloading in LLM Serving
papers.summary: KV caching reduces the serving cost of large language models (LLMs), but the growing KV cache footprint is increasingly exceeds GPU and host-memory capacity. Therefore, people use SSD to expand the KV cache storage capacity with high I/O bandwidth. However, in production LLM workload, such as multi-round conversation and LLM agents, the total amount of KV cache writes significantly exceeds SSD capacity, shortening SSD lifetime from years to months. To improve SSD lifetime, a natural solution is to reduce the KV cache writes by gating the KV cache writes via historical access patterns. However, that significantly lowers the KV cache hit rate (and increase the LLM serving cost) since KV caches from different attention types might have identical historical access pattern but different future access patterns. Our insight is that, to reduce KV cache writes without hurting KV cache hit rate, one need to not only consider the access pattern, but also application-level information such as the attention type of KV cache. Leveraging this observation, we propose Gandalf , the first SSD KV cache offloading system with SSD life time awareness. Gandalf prioritize the admission of full-attention KV cache into SSD over the cache generated by other types of attention, which significantly increases SSD lifetime without sacrificing cache hit rate. Our evaluation shows that Gandalf extends the SSD lifetime by 7.3X on average, while having negligible impact on cache hit rate across multiple workload traces and wide range of hardware capacity. Gandalf design can be extended to other flash-based storage, such as High Bandwidth Flash (HBF).

papers.title: TopoMap: A Feature-based Discriminator of the Topographical Regions in the Test Input Space

papers.title: Rethinking Post-hoc Debiasing of Large Pretrained Models
papers.summary: Large pretrained models such as CLIP are widely used as frozen feature extractors. Specifically, cross-class training pairs placed closest together by the frozen encoder almost always share a spurious attribute, regardless of the bias type, without requiring access to the bias labels. Based on this, we propose a novel approach to identify such pairs and learn a single linear map that transforms the features to perform post-hoc debiasing. The proposed approach achieves competitive performance across all datasets without access to bias attribute annotations or any LLMs.

papers.title: When Should We Intervene at Test Time?
papers.summary: Test-time adaptation helps a deployed model respond to changing inputs, but the same intervention can rescue one batch and damage the next. Updating normalization statistics, for example, can improve corrupted images yet fail when a batch contains mostly one class. Average accuracy hides these failures and cannot tell a model when to use an intervention. Target labels can guide this decision, but they are scarce and some choices are already clear. We introduce PORTAL, a controller that chooses when to deploy an intervention, which inputs to label, and when to stop querying. Each available prediction rule is a candidate, and its predictions are fixed before current feedback arrives. Every acquired label therefore evaluates all candidates on the same input. PORTAL combines these shared comparisons and directs queries toward candidates that can still overtake the current leader. It stops when the remaining labels cannot change the choice or when the possible accuracy gain no longer justifies another query. Our analysis links the required feedback to accuracy gaps and shared mistakes, explaining why some choices need much less evidence. Experiments show that this control turns an intervention that loses accuracy overall into a useful choice on selected batches. It prevents severe failures caused by changes in arrival order and preserves gains across complete corruption streams. When a fixed rule already works well, PORTAL uses little feedback to retain its performance. Periodic label checks reveal when past evidence needs refreshing and help the controller recover as conditions change. The acquired labels also train stronger candidates for future batches, and selection brings nearly all of their accuracy gains into deployment. The same feedback therefore improves both the choice made now and the predictions available to later batches.

papers.title: A Tight 3-Approximation for Fair $k$-Means
papers.summary: Fairness in clustering has attracted sustained research interest, motivated by the need to ensure equitable representation of protected groups in machine learning applications. We study fair $k$-means clustering in Euclidean space, where the proportion of each protected group in every cluster must lie within specified lower and upper bounds. The merge is cheap only when the small clusters do not move points away from their optimal centers, so we add a displacement penalty to the split, which charges each point for how far the small clusters move it. With a PTAS as the subroutine, the approximation ratio becomes $3+O(ε)$, improving the previous factor of $5+O(ε)$. This ratio is the best possible: unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves the ratio $3-δ$ for any fixed $δ>0$, even in one dimension. The solution satisfies all fairness constraints exactly and can be rounded to an integral assignment with a bounded additive violation of fairness and no increase in cost. papers.title: Spectral Braids: A Topological Descriptor for Dynamic Directed Networks
papers.summary: Eigenvalues are a workhorse of graph machine learning: spectral clustering, spectral graph neural networks, and graph kernels all summarize a network by the eigenvalues of a matrix. These eigenvalues are almost always treated as a static list of numbers. When a graph changes, however, its eigenvalues move, and when the matrix is not symmetric, they move in the complex plane, where they can wind around each other. The pattern of this winding is a braid, a classical object from topology. We propose spectral braids, a methodology for dynamic directed networks: each snapshot is aggregated into a community-level transition matrix, its complex eigenvalues are tracked over time, and the braid they trace is read off as a word. The word is then mapped to a matrix by the Burau representation, which gives a fixed-size feature vector for any classifier. The braid has a concrete meaning: each eigenvalue describes how a group of communities behaves, and each crossing records one group overtaking another. We evaluate the method on dynamic network classification, using synthetic networks of online communities whose labels describe how the network evolved between the same starting and ending states. Our experimental results show that the proposed features reach 97.1% accuracy on four classes, against 44.5% for the best feature set that does not track eigenvalues, and that the Burau features also separate networks containing the same events in a different order, which simple counts of crossings cannot do. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that defines braids and braid monodromy on graph data and uses them as features for learning on dynamic networks.

papers.summary: Multivariate time series forecasting requires capturing temporal dependencies across multiple scales while accounting for both shared and variable-specific dynamics. papers.title: An Input Skip Can Reparameterize a VAE Without Improving the Generator
papers.summary: An input skip can reduce reconstruction error while leaving a model's distribution of new samples unchanged. For a Gaussian variational autoencoder (VAE) with constant input skip $0\leqα<1$, a model without a skip can be written in skip form by multiplying its decoder output by $b=1-α$ and its noise variance by $b^2$. The distribution of observations and latent variables and its exact generative scores stay the same, while reconstruction mean squared error (MSE) is multiplied by $b^2$. Separate training can produce different generators because optimization depends on the parameter coordinates. In a Gaussian experiment with known density, changing skip and observation variance together reduces MSE but worsens energy score and the estimate of negative log density from importance sampling. On seven annual Deep-ocean Assessment and Reporting of Tsunamis (DART) records, energy score differences at the same observation variance have both signs on four original records and favor the skip on three records from 2018. Probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA) has lower mean energy scores than every neural DART fit. With the encoder and decoder kept the same, estimating observation variance from training reconstruction error can also worsen energy score. Assessing generation requires more than reconstruction error.

papers.title: CRISP: Co-designing Pruning and Scheduling for Efficient MoE Inference on Edge Servers
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on memory-constrained edge platforms is often dominated by expert-weight movement rather than computation. CRISP reorders neurons by importance so one stored expert can support multiple execution widths, assigns differentiated execution to hot, warm, and cold combinations based on frequency and expert role, and exploits heterogeneous widths to overlap expert loading with computation. Across Mixtral-8x7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B, CRISP improves throughput by up to $2.1\times$ at the same memory budget while limiting accuracy loss to 3.6\% relative to full-width inference. Our results highlight that efficient edge MoE serving requires jointly optimizing which expert capacity is preserved and how expert execution is scheduled.

papers.title: Phases of Muon: When Muon Eclipses SignSGD
papers.summary: Muon and related spectral optimizers have recently demonstrated strong empirical performance as scalable stochastic methods, often outperforming Adam. Yet their behavior remains poorly understood. We analyze stochastic Muon, which orthogonalizes an exponential moving average of minibatch gradients, on a high-dimensional matrix-valued least squares problem, and we compare it with stochastic SignSGD, a simple baseline comparable to Adam. We derive explicit deterministic dynamics that provide a tractable framework for studying learning behavior. We show that Muon has non-linear sensitivity to the effective batch $B_{\rm eff}=B(1+β)/(1-β)$. With exact whitening and small $B_{\rm eff}$ Muon fails to resolve smaller eigenmodes, slowing down convergence. Momentum and finite Newton--Shulz iterations can act as a ridge which lessen this effect. This behavior is in contrast with SignSGD which has no transition, leading to different optimal learning rates, but with matching convergence rate up to a constant factor in the isotropic setting. For anisotropic data, large batch setting Muon performs a square-root preconditioning with respect to the data covariance spectrum while SignSGD provides no preconditioning for generic covariances. We analyze time to target loss in a power law covariance model and derive a phase diagram in the data exponent $α$ and target exponent $ζ$. Muon is favored for steep covariance spectra with rich targets ($α>2$, $ζ<α+1$), SignSGD is favored for flat spectra ($α<1$), and in other regions the winner depends on how the target loss scales with dimension. Our results shed light on why replacing Adam with Muon is not trivial even from a pure optimization perspective.

papers.title: How Many and How Much? Contrastive Learning with Negative Samples for Knowledge Graph Embedding
papers.summary: Knowledge graph embedding (KGE), a fundamental technique for knowledge-centric Web and KG-augmented AI applications, is commonly trained through contrastive learning with negative samples to learn discriminative representations. Despite its empirical success, two crucial questions regarding negative samples remain underexplored: (Q1) how many negative samples should be used for each positive sample and (Q2) how much should each negative sample contribute to learning? To answer these questions, we propose RADAR, a novel contrastive learning framework for KGE models with two effective strategies, respectively: (1) Risk-aware negative budget allocation quantifies false-negative sampling risk by modeling an open-world KG as a stochastic partial observation of its closed-world counterpart and adaptively assigns a negative budget to each positive sample based on its risk; (2) Distribution-calibrated negative weighting assigns negative weights by calibrating the weighting strength for each positive based on two complementary characteristics of the negative-score distribution: dispersion and concentration. Extensive experiments on 3 real-world KGs with 4 KGE models reveal that RADAR achieves the best KGE performance on average across all model--KG combinations and reduces sampled false negatives by over 90% compared with conventional fixed-budget methods.

papers.title: The Geometry of Manifold Learning: Singular foliations via Deep Learning models
papers.summary: Deep learning algorithms have become widely used and successful across a wide range of tasks. A key challenge is determining whether these algorithms truly capture the intrinsic geometry of their training data in order to better understand what they learn from data. This new geometric structure is a foliation and the main focus of this work is to explore the non-smooth case of ReLU activation functions, where traditional geometric tools often fail. The foliation is defined through a distribution spanned by the columns of the DIM. We first prove that this distribution is non-smooth in the sense of distributions, rendering the existence of an associated foliation much more complex. To circumvent this issue, we introduce a smoothed version of this distribution that differs from the original only on a set of measure zero. Finally, we prove that this smoothed distribution induces a singular foliation on the data space, which is based on the data the network has been trained with. Our theoretical contributions provide a geometric framework to better understand how neural networks organize their input space in non-smooth settings, bridging differential geometry and deep learning theory.

papers.title: Geometric Characterisation and Structured Trajectory Surrogates for Clinical Dataset Condensation
papers.summary: Dataset condensation constructs compact synthetic datasets that retain the training utility of large real-world datasets, enabling efficient model development and potentially supporting downstream research in governed domains such as healthcare. These surrogates are optimised to reduce average loss along the path while replacing broad SGD-derived supervision with a more structured, lower-rank signal that is better aligned with the optimisation constraints of a fixed synthetic dataset, and they substantially reduce trajectory storage. These results indicate that effective trajectory matching depends on structuring the supervision signal rather than reproducing stochastic optimisation paths.

papers.title: Low-degree polynomials lower bounds for clustering in small dimension
papers.summary: We study the computational limits of clustering $n$ observations drawn from a mixture of $K$ isotropic distributions in $\mathbb R^d$, in the regime where the number $K$ of groups is much larger than the dimension $d$. This construction ensures that the moment tensors of the observations coincide with those of the uniform distribution on $\{-1,1\}^d$ up to the order $2m+1$. For any fixed $m$, we establish a low-degree polynomial lower bound showing that clustering is hard as long as the separation $Δ$ satisfies $Δ^2\ll(K^2d^{3/2}/n)^{1/(2m+2)}\wedge\sqrt d$, up to polylogarithmic factors. In particular, with a polylogarithmic separation, low-degree polynomials require $n\gtrsim K^2d^{3/2}$ observations, up to polylogarithmic factors. Through a Gaussianization argument, this hardness carries over, in the sense of reductions, to isotropic Gaussian mixtures. Our proof relies on a family of polynomials of the observations, indexed by bipartite graphs, which is almost orthonormal. The moments of these polynomials are governed by the number of solutions of polynomial systems over the finite field $\mathbb F\_{d+1}$ that are induced by the BCH code, and the crux of our analysis is to connect the combinatorial structure of the bipartite graphs with the structure of the solution sets of these systems.

papers.title: On the Sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization: Weight Disentanglement in the NTK Regime
papers.summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has been widely adopted for aligning language models with human preferences. papers.title: Discovering quantum phenomena with Interpretable Machine Learning
papers.summary: Interpretable machine learning techniques are becoming essential tools for extracting physical insights from complex quantum data. We build on recent advances in variational autoencoders to demonstrate that such models can learn physically meaningful and interpretable representations from a broad class of unlabeled quantum datasets. From raw measurement data alone, the learned representation reveals rich information about the underlying structure of quantum phase diagrams. We further augment the learning pipeline with symbolic methods, enabling the discovery of compact analytical descriptors that serve as order parameters for the distinct regimes emerging in the learned representations. We demonstrate the framework on experimental Rydberg-atom snapshots, classical shadows of the cluster Ising model, and hybrid discrete-continuous fermionic data, revealing previously unreported phenomena such as a corner-ordering pattern in the Rydberg arrays. These results establish a general framework, which constitutes an important step toward the autonomous discovery of physical descriptors from diverse quantum datasets. All methods are available through qdisc, an open-source Python library designed to make these tools accessible to the broader community.

papers.title: Gaussian Process Bandits for Constraint Black Box Lever Optimization
papers.summary: Optimizing discrete allocation weights across competing segments of a shared budget is a fundamental challenge in resource-constrained, sequential decision-making environments. In practice, this optimization is often hindered by delayed, noisy, and aggregate feedback, alongside strict operational constraints on how frequently weights can be adjusted. Because of the resulting combinatorial action space and extreme data sparsity, classical multi-armed bandit algorithms that evaluate arms independently are rendered highly inefficient. To overcome these limitations, we propose a segmentation-agnostic approach utilizing Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (GP-UCB) algorithms. By placing a Gaussian Process prior on the reward function, our method effectively shares information across neighboring configurations, drastically reducing the necessary exploration horizon. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theoretical bandit research and production-scale deployment. We first introduce a high-fidelity synthetic simulator to evaluate various kernel configurations under stationary, drifting, and reactive environments, identifying a composite Matérn + Linear kernel as the most robust choice for overcoming local noise and global shifts. Finally, we validate our findings through a large-scale Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) in a live production environment. Our empirical results demonstrate that the GP-UCB approach delivers a statistically significant efficiency lift compared to a standard $\varepsilon$-greedy baseline, offering a highly practical solution for real-world black-box lever optimization.
